paragraphs: Insufficient evidence: the National Bureau of Statistics' 2025 industry wage bulletin was checked, but no mainland China national wage distribution for this precise occupation was established. Industry averages, historical job offers, and U.S. wages are not used to fill the gap. This page corresponds to U.S. O*NET-SOC 51-9071.00; production or repair results are checked against designs, specifications, materials, and records. Occupational tasks include appraisal, but this does not mean every worker has appraisal, signing, or valuation authority.

Taking responsibility for judgments | Fit depends on whether you can do three things within the same assignment: produce and repair sound work (design to drawings or requirements, select and purchase materials, cut and file, set and assemble, polish and electroplate, inspect against specifications, record weights and work time, and produce reviewable pieces and work records); manage precision and safety (follow standards and organizational policies for precious metal and gemstone counts and custody, heat treatment and chemical bath safety, dust and ventilation, tool and equipment use, and appraisal and valuation grounds); and accept clearly defined job responsibilities (take responsibility for your production quality and appraisal grounds, and seek guidance or refer valuation conclusions, authenticity determinations, or client funds matters beyond authority). Test this through a verifiable exercise, such as preparing a piece's design explanation and process records using entirely fictional materials and drawings, rather than relying only on an interest questionnaire.

Editorial trial | Complete the fictional pendant P paper exercise below: check hole diameter, tolerances, weight disposition, and stone identification. The path section provides reference answers, a recalculation of 96 fictional units, four work samples, and a seven-day plan. Do not operate heat equipment or chemicals or handle real valuables.

Fit signals | Work activities in O*NET 51-9071.00 primarily involve creative thinking, controlling machines and processes, obtaining information, making decisions and solving problems, and inspecting equipment and materials. If you are willing to spend long periods on fine manual work, show great patience with dimensions and appearance, document work to specifications, and follow material and operational safety requirements, these daily requirements may align with your working style. Interest and personality tools are only for designing trials; they cannot determine hiring eligibility or performance.

Insufficient evidence: the National Bureau of Statistics' 2025 industry wage bulletin was checked, but no mainland China national wage distribution for this precise occupation was established. Industry averages, historical job offers, and U.S. wages are not used to fill the gap. Jewelers and precious stone and metal workers correspond to O*NET-SOC 51-9071.00: designing, making, adjusting, repairing, or appraising jewelry, gold, silver, other precious metals, or gemstones. Deliverables may include pieces, specification checks, weight and time records, and handover records. This page's workflow synthesizes tasks; verify actual processes and authority for each role. Current U.S. national pay: a 2025 median of $52,540 per year; employment of 32,800 in 2025, -3% growth for 2025—2035, and 3,700 average annual openings (an overall projection, not attributed to AI). The exact occupational wage gap for China remains; industry averages are broad references only.

entries: Objects of work | Work within precision and safety boundaries with precious metals and gemstones, designs and specifications, jewelers' tools and heat-treatment and electroplating equipment, and client requirements and deadlines.

Checkable outputs | Pieces and repairs meeting specifications, material and weight records, process and work-time records, inspection and grading grounds, and delivery and handover records. Results must be traceable to designs and material sources.

Editorial workflow | Confirm designs and specifications → select and check materials → cut and shape → set and assemble → polish and inspect → document and hand over. Check specific processes for each role.

paragraphs: Key judgments | O*NET work context data show: exactness or accuracy extremely important, 78%; indoors in a controlled environment daily, 88%; face-to-face discussions daily, 72%; substantial freedom to make decisions, 71%; time pressure daily, 64%; and decisions daily, 72%. Judgments rely on designs and specifications, material and weight records, and heat-treatment and chemical bath safety requirements.

Environment and pace | Work primarily involves fine bench work and client communication: using hands continually or almost continually, 62%; sitting more than half the time, 66%; working with others extremely important, 66%; very high responsibility for others' work outcomes, 51%; workweeks exceeding 40 hours, 47%; moderate competition, 48%; exposure to contaminants at least weekly but not daily, 34%; and daily exposure to situations involving minor burns, cuts, bites, or stings, 31%. These are context responses, not percentages of people actually injured every day.

Research inputs | O*NET51-9071.00, RAC interests, and Job Zone Three; respondent education and general preparation categories are not hard requirements. Median wages in 2025 were $52,540 per year. O*NET and BLS now both show 32,800 employed in 2025, a 3% decline for 2025—2035, and 3,700 average annual openings (replacement needs). The exact Chinese wage gap remains.

The first checks concern the objects (precious metals and gemstones, designs and specifications, tools and equipment), inputs (designs and specifications, materials and sources, weight and work-time requirements, and operational safety requirements), and deliverables (pieces meeting specifications, material and weight records, inspection and grading grounds, and delivery records). Anything unverified must remain pending verification; intuition based on experience cannot replace specifications and material records.

Assess the complete workflow in four steps: check inputs (confirm designs and specifications, materials and weights, and safety conditions) → define the task (produce and appraise only within authorization) → execute and document (complete processes and inspections to standard with an audit trail) → review and escalate (stop immediately and report dimensional deviations, material or authenticity doubts, or conclusions beyond authority). A complete workflow requires verifiable specifications, materials, and authorization, rather than merely an attractive appearance.

Boundaries with neighboring roles | This page covers only the precise occupation O*NET-SOC 51-9071.00, Jewelers and Precious Stone and Metal Workers. Neighboring occupations such as craft artists, structural metal fabricators, grinding workers, metal and plastic patternmakers, and tool and die makers differ in their objects of work, authorized scope, and responsibilities. They cannot be interchanged based solely on titles, and proxy categories cannot replace organizational authorization, qualifications, or appraisal and valuation responsibility.

Craft art | Core outputs are original handmade pieces and formal expression. This occupation focuses on specification-based production and repair of precious metals and gemstones; material value and precision requirements differ, and shared manual skills do not imply identical responsibilities.

Structural metal fabrication | Core outputs are fabricated and installed structural metal components. This occupation focuses on small precision pieces; dimensional scale and safety requirements differ, so roles cannot be interchanged based only on titles.
Grinding | Core outputs are grinding and polishing to tolerances. This occupation focuses on jewelry and gemstones; objects and equipment differ substantially and must be checked separately.

Metal and plastic patternmaking | O*NET 51-4062.00 makes foundry patterns, core boxes, and templates; it does not broadly mean all models or jewelry design. Foundry objects, machine tools, and pattern inspection skills must be learned; jewelry work samples do not directly qualify someone for the role.
The objects of jewelry and precious metal work and AI boundaries: which steps may be assisted and which judgments people must remain responsible for.

Direct answer | FermatMind recommends trialing assistance with sketch explanations, weight recalculations, and anomaly summaries using fictional work orders, checking fixed inputs item by item. Do not claim efficiency gains before measuring benefits. BLS outlook discusses how 3D printing and robotic polishing may raise productivity and reduce demand; this is an industry projection, not measured generative AI adoption. AI Impact Score 25% is an editorial estimate. Model impact index for three equally weighted representative core tasks; not a measured share of working time or a job-loss probability. floor((50+0+25)/3+0.5)=25; fermatmind-ai-impact-v1; 2026-10-18.The three tasks, ratings and sources are listed in the FermatMind method source record on this page.

Evidence explanation | O*NET's hot technology page counts software mentions in full-year U.S. recruitment in 2025: Illustrator and Photoshop each 3%, Excel 1%. These are not AI adoption rates. BLS provides an automation outlook, and NIST provides general generative AI risks such as fabricated output; neither measures the actual effects of this page's paper trial.

Differences in impact | Sketches, specifications, and records support trials that can be checked against inputs; actual setting, precision inspection, and chemical baths involve physical objects, equipment, and safety. Text drafts cannot directly become process parameters, appraisal conclusions, or valuations, and software mention percentages do not demonstrate that these tasks are already automated.

Responsibility chain | From confirming designs and specifications through tool and equipment handling, human review, finished-piece inspection, and recordkeeping, every step must have a clear responsible person and traceable evidence. Appraisal and valuation conclusions must not rely solely on a model.

Turning point | First practice specification table reading, material recalculations, and deviation handovers, then compare manual and tool drafts for omissions, calculation errors, and time spent. Judge benefits from records without declaring efficiency gains in advance. Actual processes and safety release still follow organizational rules.

Editorial trial suggestion | Input this page's fictional pendant work order and ask the tool to organize specifications, weights, and anomalies. Recheck the out-of-tolerance 2.08 mm, unexplained 0.10 g, and inconsistent stone identifiers. Do not generate real alloy formulas, heat-treatment parameters, or chemical bath ratios.

Human control points | Separately check specifications against physical objects, material identifiers, equipment conditions, and inspection results. A grading report is not a valuation, and a database report match does not replace verification that it corresponds to the physical object. Heat and chemical processes must follow organizational training and product safety data.

Occupational title comparison | The Chinese title corresponds to U.S. 51-9071.00; it does not establish a Chinese occupational classification, qualification, or wage mapping. The National Bureau of Statistics' 2025 industry wage bulletin was checked; industry averages cannot be renamed this occupation's median.

Broad reference | Jewelry and silverware manufacturing duties relate to manufacturing. National Bureau of Statistics Tables 2 / 5: average annual wages of employees in urban manufacturing entities in China in 2025 were CNY 113,594 in non-private entities and CNY 76,055 in private entities. These figures are not this occupation's wage range, median, or take-home income. Source: https://www.stats.gov.cn/zwfwck/sjfb/202605/t20260515_1963707.html.

AI and pay boundaries | This page has not established causal evidence of AI's effect on this occupation's wages. Mentions of software in job advertisements, automation outlooks, and specific pay quotes require separate checks.
U.S. pay reference | O*NET 51-9071.00 national wage page, 2025 BLS OEWS, precise U.S. national occupational category; checked on 2026-10-11.

U.S. wages in 2025 | Annual wages at the 10 / 25 / 50 / 75 / 90 percentiles were $35,580 / 39,520 / 52,540 / 69,810 / 87,540 respectively, with a median of $52,540 per year. Percentiles are neither minimum wages nor experience levels; the data do not represent individual take-home income.

Pay definition | OEWS measures employees' pretax wages for regular working hours, including commissions and production bonuses, but excluding overtime premiums, nonproduction bonuses, and employer benefit costs. It does not cover self-employment income; percentiles are not starting salaries. Methodology: https://www.bls.gov/oes/current/oes_tec.htm.

Interpretation | This category helps explain the occupation's pay scale and direction of demand; it cannot serve as an individual quote or be compared directly with mainland China or any other market. Self-employment or contracted bench work may have income structures differing from employee wage statistics.

Industry definitions | The four U.S. 51-9071 industry median annual wages from BLS OOH2025 are retained. O*NET's current 2025 employment shares are 37% in retail and 16% in manufacturing; employment shares are not wage rankings or demand growth.

Influencing factors | Employer type (jewelry retail, manufacturing, repair studios, or self-employment), specialization (setting, metalwork, or gemology), region, and skill level affect actual income and its stability. The median on this page is a statistical position and does not correspond to specific experience levels.

Which interests, abilities, and working styles matter more for jewelers and precious stone and metal workers? This page discusses fit only through work samples and responsibility boundaries; personality labels do not replace judgments about qualifications or performance.

Direct answer | Fit signals include sustained fine manual work, great patience with dimensions and appearance, working from specifications and material records, and escalating appraisal or valuation doubts. Personality labels do not establish fit. Interest and personality tools can only help design trials; they cannot determine hiring eligibility, authorization, or performance.

Positive signals | You can follow procedures to cut and shape, set and assemble, polish and inspect; check materials and weights and identify dimensional and appearance deviations; and retain reviewable process and work-time records and hand work over accurately within authorization.

Caution conditions | Risk signals include skipping inspections or records to hurry, judging gemstone grades and authenticity from experience, inadequate heat-treatment or chemical bath protection, poor precious metal and gemstone counts and custody, and unauthorized valuation or authenticity conclusions. If prolonged fine work, precision pressure, and material value risks are difficult for you to tolerate, treat them as practical costs requiring serious consideration.

Exercise (FermatMind original, entirely on paper) | Fictional pendant P requires a hole diameter of 2.00±0.05 mm and finished metal weight of 3.00±0.10 g. Metal input is 4.00 g, the finished piece is 2.95 g, and recovered scrap is 0.95 g; inspection records show a 2.08 mm hole. The stone label is S and the attached report identifier is T, with no correspondence established. Simulated cost uses fictional units only: materials 60 units, labor 45 minutes × 0.8 units per minute, other costs 0. Calculate tolerances, the weight discrepancy, and cost, and list release blockers and handovers. Do not assume an allowable loss rate or infer a price from the report. Do not handle real valuables, heat equipment, chemicals, or cutting tools.

Conclusion | Activity preferences align more closely with a combination of hands-on making, artistic design, and following procedures (O*NET interest code RAC). However, interest codes can only help design trials; they cannot determine hiring eligibility or performance.

Conclusion | This page does not use a single personality label to predict jewelry work performance. Observe whether you can recalculate specifications, identify hole diameter and identifier deviations, and honestly hand over unexplained weights. Paper comprehension, trained manual performance, hiring, and actual authority require separate checks.

Conclusion | RIASEC or personality frameworks can only help formulate questions; they cannot replace work samples, learning ability, qualifications, and actual performance evidence for this occupation. No tool conclusion constitutes a hiring, authorization, or appointment decision.

Material and asset records | Weight discrepancies or handover omissions may cause asset and responsibility disputes. Suggested controls: count and record disposition and handover persons under organizational procedures; investigate unexplained discrepancies first, without inventing a universal allowable loss rate.

Process precision | Hole, dimension, or setting deviations may cause rework and quality issues. Suggested controls: review against explicit specifications and inspection conditions and record deviations; one passing item does not override another out-of-tolerance item.

Heat and chemicals | Welding fumes, ultraviolet radiation, burns, eye injuries, electric shock, and chemical exposure require controls. Suggested controls: check equipment procedures, labels / SDS, and training; the organization confirms protection and safety conditions, and anomalies stop relevant processes. This page provides no parameters or formulas.

Grading and valuation | Inconsistent material identifiers or treating grading reports as price conclusions may cause incorrect delivery. Suggested controls: GIA reports contain no valuation; Report Check only verifies archived information. Check physical correspondence, signing, and valuation authority separately, referring doubts to the organization's designated responsible person.

Rushing and escalation | Deadline pressure may cause missed inspections, missing records, or incorrect release. Suggested controls: separately register deviations, unexplained weights, and identification issues; stop relevant steps first and hand over unresolved matters without hiding anomalies under pressure.

How to become a jeweler or precious stone and metal worker: preparation, training, and a path of responsibility. Begin with metalworking fundamentals, materials and tools, setting and polishing techniques, gem fundamentals, and safety standards. Training or certificates do not automatically confer appraisal qualifications or valuation authority.

Entry reference | BLS OOH describes typical U.S. entry as high school education, though employer requirements vary. Reaching proficiency on the job often takes at least a year and depends on specialization; certification is optional. O*NET Job Zone Three is a general preparation category, not a uniform one-to-two-year requirement; check target roles' processes, supervision, and work sample requirements.

Jurisdictional checks | U.S. references are BLS entry information and OSHA hazard communication. In mainland China, check local applicable requirements, process equipment, and organizational procedures for each role. Metalworking, chemical baths, appraisal reports, and valuation require separate training and authorization checks; U.S. occupational pages or GIA methodology do not establish Chinese qualifications.

Qualification boundaries | Courses, certificates, or training do not automatically confer appraisal qualifications, valuation authority, or precious metal trading authority. Education, certificates, qualifications, hiring, organizational authorization, and signing authority are distinct statuses; specific requirements depend on the role and applicable rules.

Responsibilities by stage | At entry and trial stages, complete basic processes and records under supervision. At later stages, independently produce, repair, and inspect within job authorization, taking responsibility for precision and material records.

Reference deliverables | The hole diameter range is 1.95—2.05 mm; 2.08 exceeds the upper limit by 0.03 mm. The finished weight range is 2.90—3.10 g; 2.95 is within range. Input less the finished piece and scrap is 4.00−2.95−0.95=0.10 g unexplained, which cannot automatically be recorded as allowable loss. Labor is 36 units and total simulated cost is 96 units, not a market quote. The hole deviation, unexplained weight, and unverified S / T correspondence all require handover; the product is not released. Passing weight and correct cost calculations do not remove other blockers. Deliver four clearly fictional samples: an input / specification table, weight and cost recalculations, an inspection deviation form, and an unresolved-matters handover form. The latter lists facts, pending checks, receiving responsible persons, and review results, without physical appraisal or valuation.

Seven-day plan (20—30 minutes daily, editorial suggestion) | Day 1: copy the work order and boundaries. Day 2: calculate both tolerance ranges. Day 3: recalculate the 0.10 g discrepancy and 96-unit cost. Day 4: write the hole diameter deviation form. Day 5: write the S / T and weight unresolved-matters handover. Day 6: have a peer check the fixed inputs for arithmetic, omissions, and unauthorized release. Day 7: revise the four samples and record reasons. Passing observations are traceable inputs, reproducible calculations, and no omitted blockers among the three; paper samples do not verify actual manual proficiency or confer appraisal authority.

Neighboring directions | Before changing careers, list transferable skills (metalwork and setting, precision and inspection, material and weight records, client communication, and safety and compliance), then specify the tools, qualifications, and evidence of responsibility required for the new role. Moving into craft art, structural metal fabrication, grinding and polishing, or mold making requires the corresponding process scale and safety evidence.
Market signals and related directions for jewelers and precious stone and metal workers: this page states only observations within the coverage of its sources.

Overall U.S. employment projection, not attributed to AI | O*NET 51-9071.00: employment of 32,800 in 2025, -3% growth for 2025—2035, and 3,700 projected average annual openings (including growth and replacement needs). Insufficient evidence: a national employment projection and a standardized recruitment sample for this occupation in China were not obtained; these figures cannot be converted into individual hiring probabilities.

Employment projection | The 3% decline for BLS2025—2035 and 3,700 annual openings are entirely replacement needs from transfers or exits; O*NET now also reflects 2025 employment of 32,800 and the new opening period. Imports, 3D printing, and robotic polishing are outlook factors, not measured generative AI adoption or independent causal effects.

Transferable skills | Shared foundations in related directions include metalwork and setting, precision and inspection, material and weight records, client communication, and safety and compliance. Each path still requires the tools, qualifications, and evidence of responsibility corresponding to its new outputs and obligations.

Skill gaps | Moving into neighboring fields such as craft art, structural metal fabrication, grinding and polishing, mold making, or tool and die making requires the corresponding process scale, materials and equipment, or precision standards evidence. Proximity supports comparison of directions; it does not mean automatic job transfer or mutual recognition of qualifications.

The national wage page's 2025 percentiles are $35,580 / 39,520 / 52,540 / 69,810 / 87,540 per year; employment uses a 2025 base year and 2025—2035 projections. NBS Tables 2 / 5 support only average annual wages for China's manufacturing industry, not this occupation. AI analysis is task-level editorial judgment. The shared registry, Hero, and FAQ retain their original definitions; no claim of page-wide consistency is made.

description.text: What jewelers and precious stone and metal workers do, how to enter and train, their material and appraisal boundaries, and which tasks AI may change. This page corresponds to O*NET-SOC 51-9071.00, interest code RAC, and Job Zone Three. U.S. wages and employment use the precise O*NET / BLS occupational category; mainland China wage gaps are recorded according to the evidence.

title.text: Evaluating Jewelry and Precious Metal Work as a Career: Work, Entry, and Risk Boundaries

subject.name: Jewelers and Precious Stone and Metal Workers
subject.summary: Jewelers and precious stone and metal workers design, make, adjust, repair, or appraise jewelry, precious metals, and gemstones, delivering pieces, specification inspections, and material records. Consider manual precision, asset handover, and heat and chemical safety; grading reports are not valuations, and authority requires separate job checks. U.S. wages and employment are presented by period; evidence for Chinese national occupational wages is insufficient.
